name: ISPC (Intel Implicit SPMD Program Compiler)
language: ISPC (C-like SPMD language; compiler written in C++)
baseline: Reference serial C++ versions of the examples/ workloads (gcc 4.2.1 on OS X 10.7.2; MSVC 2010 for the 40-core table)
workload: Nine example workloads from the ispc examples/ directory (AOBench, Binomial Options, Black-Scholes, Deferred Shading, Mandelbrot, Perlin noise, ray tracer, 3D stencil, volume rendering) compared with the reference C++ implementation that ships in the same directory.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.rst, 1 core with AVX: AOBench 6.19x, Binomial Options 7.94x, Black-Scholes 8.45x, Deferred Shading 5.02x, Mandelbrot 6.21x, Perlin Noise 5.37x, Ray Tracer 4.31x, 3D Stencil 4.05x, Volume Rendering 3.60x; 4 cores: 15.53x to 33.43x. 40-core Xeon E7-8870 (SSE4): 63.85x to 243.18x. README: 'frequently provides a 3x or more speedup on architectures with 4-wide vector SSE units and 5x-6x on architectures with 8-wide AVX vector units'.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline: gcc 4.2.1 (OS X 10.7.2 distribution) flags not stated; MSVC 2010 flags not stated for the 40-core table. ispc target: AVX (iMac) and SSE4 (Xeon).
hardware: 4-core Apple iMac, 3.4GHz Intel Core-i7 (AVX); 2.40GHz 40-core Intel Xeon E7-8870 (SSE4) on Windows Server 2008 Enterprise.
tradeoffs: Kernels must be rewritten in the ispc dialect and built as a separate compile step with one object per ISA target (SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/AVX512/NEON/Xe); control-flow divergence costs lanes; calls into C/C++ through a plain C ABI.
caveats: First-party numbers from a 2011-era setup. The serial baseline is gcc 4.2.1, which is far too old to auto-vectorize with AVX, so the 1-core speedups mostly measure SIMD that the baseline compiler never emitted; baseline flags are not stated. The 4-core and 40-core columns compare multi-core ispc task code against a serial baseline, which is not like for like. No re-run on a current gcc/clang at -O3 -march=native is recorded in the doc.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/ispc/ispc README and docs/perf.rst (found via github.com/topics/ispc)
why_faster: SPMD-on-SIMD execution model: program instances map onto vector lanes (explicit vectorization the baseline compiler did not do) plus task parallelism across cores, 'without the difficulty of writing intrinsics' (README).

name: SimdNBodyKernels (ispc n-body kernels)
baseline: Scalar serial C++ kernel in the same repo (nbody_serial.cpp, built as x87 code)
workload: Direct O(N^2) n-body force summation: grav3Daccel and vortex3Dvel kernels with 10000, 20000 or 50000 particles, serial versus ispc SIMD and SIMD plus threads.
claimed_speedup: grav3Daccel SIMD vs serial: 6.79x (i5-2467M, AVX), 8.01x (Xeon E5-2640, AVX), 14.03x (i7-5960X, AVX2); vortex3Dvel: 7.06x, 8.15x, 10.95x; vortex3Dvel_mt1d (SIMD plus threads): 12.45x, 86.49x, 88.10x.
compiler_and_flags: llvm/clang 3.5.0 (laptop, desktop) and 3.4.2 (server) with ispc; optimization flags not listed in the README.
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 licensed (copyleft); needs the ispc toolchain; structure-of-arrays data layout; single-step O(N^2) kernels only, no tree codes.
caveats: The README says the serial baseline is the 'X87' build of the same source, so it is not an autovectorized SSE/AVX C++ baseline; a modern gcc/clang -O3 -march=native build would narrow the gap. Cycle counts are reported in mcycles, no wall-clock time. Compiler flags for the serial build are not stated. Old compilers (clang 3.4/3.5) and hardware.
why_faster: Same kernel source compiled by ispc for SIMD (SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/FMA3) with runtime dispatch, versus the serial x87 build.

name: Halide
language: C++ (embedded DSL and compiler; Python bindings)
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C/C++, x86 intrinsics and CUDA implementations of image-processing pipelines (PLDI 2013 paper)
workload: Image-processing pipelines (the PLDI 2013 evaluation includes local Laplacian filters, a 99-stage graph) rewritten as short Halide programs and compared with expert implementations.
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2013 abstract (as quoted by a web search result, paper not opened): performance 'up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics, and CUDA implementations optimized by experts over weeks or months'.
tradeoffs: Separate algorithm and schedule: good schedules need tuning or an autoscheduler; ahead-of-time or JIT compile step; C++ and Python front ends; mainly array and image workloads.
caveats: Snippet only: the PLDI 2013 PDF (people.csail.mit.edu, commit.csail.mit.edu) was not reachable from this environment, so the 5x figure is the best case across applications, not a per-benchmark number, and baseline compiler/flags/CPU are unverified. A secondary write-up in the same search result reports local Laplacian at 158 ms (79 lines of Halide) against 335 ms (262 lines of C++/OpenMP); not verified. The Halide repo README itself carries no performance numbers. 2012-2013 baselines. The paper-based retier belongs to the papers search.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/halide; WebSearch 'Halide PLDI 2013 local Laplacian bilateral grid faster than hand-tuned C++'
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule so the compiler/user can trade parallelism, locality and recomputation (tiling, fusion, vectorization) per pipeline; mechanism taken from the paper title, paper not opened.

name: Halide hannk (Halide-based TFLite-compatible inference runtime)
workload: Single-inference latency of quantized uint8 TFLite models (Inception v1-v4, MobileNet v1/v2) on an x86 laptop with AVX2 and on a Pixel 4 Cortex-A76 core.
claimed_speedup: x86 OSX laptop with AVX2: 2.49x to 3.11x (inception_v1_224_quant 72.5 ms TFLite vs 28.4 ms Halide, 2.55x; mobilenet_v2_1.0_224_quant 30.6 vs 9.85 ms, 3.11x). Snapdragon 855 A76 core (Pixel 4): 0.99x to 1.54x (inception_v1_224_quant 24.7 vs 25.0 ms, 0.99x; mobilenet_v1_0.25_128_quant 0.97 vs 0.63 ms, 1.54x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; TensorFlow v2.5.0 build configuration not stated.
hardware: 'x86 OSX laptop w/ AVX2' (CPU model not stated); Qualcomm Snapdragon 855 A76 core (Pixel 4).
stars_or_usage: Part of halide/Halide (6.6k stars); the README calls hannk a work in progress
tradeoffs: Only quantized uint8 networks supported; multicore parallelism and Hexagon HVX still on the TODO list; Halide JIT/AOT build dependency.
caveats: First-party table from 2021 against TensorFlow 2.5.0, the latest release when written. last_commit is the repo-level date, not the hannk folder. Gap is mostly gone on the Pixel 4 (0.99x to 1.54x). The README says multicore parallelism is still TODO, so thread counts for both sides are unclear. CPU model of the laptop is not stated.

name: llama2.mojo
baseline: llama2.c (karpathy/llama2.c, OpenMP build); also llama.cpp CPU
workload: CPU inference of llama2 models (TinyStories 15M/42M/110M and TinyLlama-1.1B) in tokens per second, multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: README: 'outperforms the original llama2.c by 30% in multi-threaded inference' and llama.cpp on baby-llama CPU inference by 20%. Tables (llama2.c OMP vs llama2.mojo, tok/s): Mac M1 Max, 8 workers: stories15M 730 vs 1283, stories42M 270 vs 506, stories110M 102 vs 218; 4 vCPU Xeon Skylake VM (-j 4): 292 vs 327, 117 vs 150, 53 vs 66, TinyLlama-1.1B 5.2 vs 6.8; Core i7-8700: stories15M 435 vs 440, stories110M 64 vs 63, TinyLlama 7.25 vs 7.25 (parity).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0 (persistent worker pool build); llama2.c compiler and flags not stated, only OMP threads (4 threads on the Xeon VM).
hardware: Apple M1 Max (8 workers); 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Skylake AVX-512 VM (Ubuntu 26.04); Intel Core i7-8700 @ 3.20GHz (Ubuntu 20.04).
tradeoffs: Needs the Mojo toolchain and MAX (parallelize), and tracks Mojo releases closely (updated for Mojo 1.1); single-file inference tool, not a general tensor library.
caveats: Self-run benchmark; llama2.c compile flags (e.g. -Ofast or runfast, -march) are not stated. Advantage varies by machine: 1.76x on the M1 Max (derived from page data, stories15M 1283/730), about 1.12x to 1.31x on the Xeon VM (derived), and parity on the i7-8700. llama2.c is a deliberately minimal reference, not a tuned inference engine. A separate 'extensive benchmark' page on engiware.com was not opened.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/mojo listing; WebSearch 'Mojo faster than C benchmark github llama2.mojo'
why_faster: README: the Mojo version 'leverages Mojo's SIMD & vectorization primitives' and parallelizes the matmul (explicit SIMD plus a worker pool) instead of relying on C compiler auto-vectorization.

name: llm.mojo (Mojo port of llm.c, CPU)
baseline: llm.c train_gpt2.c (karpathy/llm.c, with and without OpenMP)
workload: Average GPT-2 training-loop time on CPU (train_gpt2.mojo vs train_gpt2.c), M2 MacBook Pro, OpenMP run with 10 threads.
claimed_speedup: train_gpt2.mojo 1704 ms per loop (150 tok/s) vs train_gpt2.c with OpenMP 1987 ms (128 tok/s), about 1.17x (derived from page data); train_gpt2.c without OpenMP 7405 ms (34 tok/s).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0; C compiler and flags for train_gpt2.c not stated; OMP_NUM_THREADS=10.
tradeoffs: Needs Mojo 1.0 and max 26.5.0 (pinned in pixi.toml); CPU only; the README says no concrete plans to develop it further.
caveats: README states the figures are 'a general comparison rather than precise, repeatable metrics'. It ports an early-2024 llm.c commit (2d43e5b); the README notes upstream llm.c has since optimized its CPU matmul with register tiling, so the baseline is stale. The project's stated aim is matching C performance, so the 1.17x edge is within what thread settings could change. C compiler and flags not stated.
found_via: WebSearch 'Mojo faster than C benchmark github llama2.mojo OR matmul' result snippet, then github.com/dorjeduck/llm.mojo

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (SciMLBenchmarks ODE solver work-precision results)
baseline: Sundials CVODE/ARKODE (C), Hairer dopri5/dop853/radau (Fortran, via ODEInterface) and LSODA, as driven from the SciMLBenchmarks suite
metric: other (work-precision efficiency: run time at matched error)
workload: Work-precision diagrams for non-stiff ODEs, stiff ODEs (including the large Filament PDE) and dynamical ODEs in the SciMLBenchmarks.jl suite.
claimed_speedup: No single factor on the README page. Summary text: for non-stiff ODEs 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl's methods are the most efficient by a good amount', the Vern methods do best in every benchmark of the category, and ARKODE and Hairer's dopri5/dop853 are 'far less efficient than the Vern methods'; for stiff ODEs the OrdinaryDiffEq.jl KenCarp4 is 'much more efficient' than ARKODE in most cases (ARKODE 'very inconsistent', often diverges), while lsoda is among the most efficient on small stiff problems at high tolerances and radau wins at 1e-13.
compiler_and_flags: Julia package manifests per benchmark; C/Fortran solver build flags not stated in the README.
hardware: Workstation with AMD EPYC 7502 32-core 2.50GHz (official benchmark machine), run on self-hosted AMD EPYC CI runners.
tradeoffs: Julia runtime and compile latency; competitor solvers are driven through Julia wrapper packages; stiff-solver ranking is problem dependent.
caveats: First-party suite (the SciML authors run it), with only qualitative rankings on the README page; the numeric work-precision plots live in the separate SciMLBenchmarksOutput repo, which was not opened. The compared methods are largely different algorithms (Vern/Tsit5/KenCarp4 against dopri5/ARKODE), so this is a method-quality win rather than a language-codegen win. The C/Fortran libraries are not the strongest possible baselines for every problem class (README itself lists cases where lsoda and radau win).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl README (found while checking Julia packages for explicit C/Fortran baselines)

name: TriangularSolve.jl
baseline: Intel MKL triangular solve (trsm) called through Julia LinearAlgebra rdiv!/ldiv! (libmkl_rt.so loaded via MKL.jl on the Intel run); BLAS on the M1 run not named
workload: 100x100 Float64 triangular solves with 100 right-hand sides (rdiv! UpperTriangular, ldiv! LowerTriangular), median of 10000 samples, single and multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: Medians, i7-1165G7 single thread: rdiv! 17.916 us vs MKL 19.852 us (1.11x derived from page data), ldiv! 19.694 us vs 21.561 us (1.09x derived); 8 threads: rdiv! 8.769 us vs 14.163 us (1.62x derived), ldiv! 9.871 us vs 15.258 us (1.55x derived); M1 single thread: rdiv! 21.624 us vs 46.166 us (2.14x derived), ldiv! 34.375 us vs 49.124 us (1.43x derived; a second run in the README shows 23.875 us).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.8.0-DEV.438 (LLVM 12.0.1, tigerlake target), JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8; no compile flags (Julia JIT); BLAS.set_num_threads(1) for the single-thread run.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz (Linux); Apple M1 Mac (single-threaded only).
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; part of the JuliaSIMD/LoopVectorization ecosystem
tradeoffs: Only Float32/Float64 with at least two right-hand sides, and the README says only rdiv! with UpperTriangular and ldiv! with LowerTriangular are the supported configurations on the benchmarked paths; vector right-hand sides use pure-Julia sweeps.
caveats: Single matrix size (N=100) from the author's README, run in 2021 on a Julia dev build; MKL is closed-source and hand-tuned (not a C/C++ -O3 baseline), the single-thread advantage on Intel is only about 10%, and the M1 BLAS backend is not named. The README does not give a mechanism. Tier A rests on the README code plus versioninfo (CPU, Julia and LLVM versions), but it is author-run.
found_via: GitHub: JuliaSIMD package pages checked for BLAS comparisons

name: Fortran (gfortran) in plb2: matmul
baseline: C matmul in the same suite (Clang 15.0.0, CFLAGS -O3 -fwrapv -flto)
workload: plb2 matmul: naive O(n^3) multiplication of two 1500x1500 double matrices, elapsed time measured with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: matmul column: Fortran f90:gcc (GCC 13.2.0) 0.51 vs C c:clang (Clang 15.0.0) 0.54, about 1.06x (derived from page data). The same table shows Fortran slower than C on nqueen (2.67 vs 2.57) and sudoku (1.84 vs 1.56).
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran -O3 (src/fortran/Makefile); C: -O3 -fwrapv -flto (src/c/Makefile); Fortran GCC 13.2.0, C Clang 15.0.0.
tradeoffs: CC0 dedication carries no patent grant. gfortran and Clang are different compiler backends.
caveats: plb2 makes no claim that Fortran beats C; this row is read off the timing table. The 6% margin is on one run on one machine, and different compilers (gfortran vs Clang) and loop layouts are compared: the C code uses double** rows with i-k-j loops, the Fortran code uses contiguous column-major arrays with j-k-i loops. Time unit is not stated on the README table. The source gives no mechanism, which caps the tier at C. Julia (0.76) and Mojo (1.12) are slower than C on the same benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: attractivechaos/plb2 README results table, src/fortran/matmul.F90, src/c/matmul.c and Makefiles

name: Julia (no BLAS) in kostya/benchmarks: Matmul
baseline: C/gcc and C/clang matmul in the same suite (gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8, -O3 -march=native -flto=auto)
workload: kostya Matmul: allocate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices, median of repeated runs.
claimed_speedup: Matmul table: Julia (no BLAS) 1.113 s vs C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, about 2.7x (derived from page data). Julia with BLAS: 0.170 s (threads: 1), 0.120 s (threads: 2), but C++/g++ with Eigen is 0.081 s, faster than every Julia row.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G, Docker image Debian forky/sid
stars_or_usage: star count not shown on the pages opened
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up time and about 256 MiB baseline memory per the table.
caveats: Not a like-for-like language comparison. The Julia 'no BLAS' source (matmul/matmul.jl) uses Threads.@threads with @simd ivdep and @fastmath on an axpy-style loop, while the C source is single-threaded and sums a dot product with no -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize the reduction; the thread count of the Julia run is not confirmed (no -t flag in JULIA_RUN). The suite README does not claim Julia beats C, and the kostya table's own C++/g++ Eigen row (0.081 s) is about 37x faster than the C row (derived from page data). Source gives no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README Matmul table, matmul/matmul.jl, matmul/matmul.c, common/commands.mk

name: Futhark
baseline: Hand-written CUDA/OpenCL reference implementations of the published benchmarks that futhark-benchmarks ports (Rodinia, Parboil, FinPar, PBBS, XSBench and others)
workload: Data-parallel array programs compiled to CPU or GPU backends; futhark-benchmarks holds the ported benchmark programs.
tradeoffs: Purely functional ML-family language; programs are rewritten in Futhark and called from C, Python or other hosts through generated code; sequential/irregular code does not fit.
caveats: No numbers on any page opened: the README says only that Futhark 'can be compiled to typically very efficient parallel code, running on either a CPU or GPU'. The futhark-benchmarks README gives no results or hardware. The numeric comparisons live in papers and futhark-lang.org/performance.html, which were not reachable here (host not resolvable). A web search snippet of a 2026 arXiv paper reports Futhark big-integer multiplication about 1.35x slower than hand-coded CUDA, i.e. parity-or-slower, not faster. Tier D slot used because the project is notable (more than 1k stars); needs a paper-based retier.
